title: Corruption in health systems: An umbrella review of the pathways to health, financial, and social outcomes
content:
by Michele Coleman, Petra Varkonyi, Martin McKee, Neil Spicer, Max Wybrant, Dina Balabanova

Corruption in health systems is increasingly perceived to undermine governance, equity, and service delivery, posing a major barrier to achieving universal health coverage and the Sustainable Development Goals. To fill the evidence gap, this umbrella review synthesises findings from twelve systematic reviews and meta-analyses to examine how health-sector corruption affects health, financial, and social outcomes. It identifies common types of corruption, including substandard and falsified medicines (SFM), informal payments, absenteeism, pharmaceutical promotion, procurement fraud, and billing abuse, and maps the pathways by which they affect outcomes. The review reveals two recurring dynamics: incentives arising from systemic vulnerabilities and opportunities created by governance failures. SFM contribute to avoidable mortality and economic strain, particularly in low-resource settings. Informal payments and absenteeism disproportionately affect poor and rural populations, eroding trust and deepening inequities. The pharmaceutical industry’s influence distorts prescribing practices, raising costs and compromising care quality. Findings suggest that isolated interventions are insufficient. Effective anti-corruption strategies must reduce incentives through fair pay and adequate resources, close off opportunities via digitalisation and process reform, and strengthen accountability through independent oversight and transparency. The review also underscores the need for improved economic modelling and data quality to quantify the burden of corruption better. Despite limitations, including reliance on secondary sources and heterogeneity across studies, this synthesis provides a system-level framework for understanding corruption’s impact and guiding targeted, context-sensitive reforms. It contributes to the Lancet Global Health Commission on Anti-Corruption in Health’s efforts to advance transparency, accountability, and health equity.
